facts.fact_text: The applicant is a vice-president of Zelyonka (Зелёнка), a non-governmental youth organisation.

On 17 March 2009 the applicant, acting on behalf of Zelyonka, notified the Odessa City Mayor of the organisation's intention to hold a peaceful assembly (picket) in front of the Odessa City Council building on 19 March 2009 from 11 a.m. to 1 p.m.

On 17 March 2009 the applicant, acting on behalf of Zelyonka, notified the Head of the Prymorsky District Police Department of Odessa of the organisation's intention to hold a peaceful assembly (picket) in front of the Odessa City Council building on 19 March 2009 from 11 a.m. to 1 p.m.

The declared purpose of the planned assembly on 19 March 2009 was to demand the completion of the construction of residential buildings contracted by the Odessa City Council's Department of Construction.
The picket took place as planned between 11 a.m. and 1 p.m. on 19 March 2009.
According to the applicant, the picket on 19 March 2009 was peaceful.
According to the applicant, only a few people took part in the picket on 19 March 2009.
The police report of 19 March 2009 noted that about 250 persons had taken part in the picket.
The police report of 19 March 2009 noted that there had been no violation of public order during the picket.
On 4 April 2009 a police officer of the Prymorsky District Police Department of Odessa drew up an administrative offence report in the applicant's presence.
The administrative offence report of 4 April 2009 indicated that on 19 March 2009 the applicant had organised and held a picket in violation of Article 185-1 of the Code of Administrative Offences.

The administrative offence report of 4 April 2009 indicated that on 19 March 2009 the applicant had organised and held a picket in violation of the decision of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine of 19 April 2001.
The administrative offence report of 4 April 2009 was referred to a court.
On 15 May 2009 the Prymorsky District Court of Odessa examined the applicant's case.
According to the record of the hearing provided by the Government, the questioning at the Prymorsky District Court of Odessa on 15 May 2009 took place between 1.24 and 1.34 p.m.
After the questioning on 15 May 2009, the judge of the Prymorsky District Court of Odessa retired to the deliberations chamber.
At 2.27 p.m. on 15 May 2009 the judge of the Prymorsky District Court of Odessa publicly pronounced judgment.
The hearing at the Prymorsky District Court of Odessa on 15 May 2009 closed at 2.32 p.m.
According to the Government, the full text of the judgment of the Prymorsky District Court of Odessa of 15 May 2009 was pronounced publicly.

According to the Government, three hours after the judgment of 15 May 2009 was pronounced, the court clerk of the Prymorsky District Court of Odessa handed a hard copy of the judgment to the applicant's representative.

According to the applicant, the judgment of the Prymorsky District Court of Odessa of 15 May 2009 was not pronounced in public but given to his representative in writing three hours after the end of the hearing.

In its judgment of 15 May 2009, the Prymorsky District Court of Odessa found that the applicant had violated public order by failing to give the Odessa City Council sufficient advance notification of the picket he had organised.
In its judgment of 15 May 2009, the Prymorsky District Court of Odessa found the applicant guilty of having violated the procedure for organising and holding meetings and demonstrations.
In its judgment of 15 May 2009, the Prymorsky District Court of Odessa fined the applicant 170 Ukrainian hryvnias (UAH) (approximately 17 euros (EUR)).
On 25 May 2009 the applicant appealed against the judgment of the Prymorsky District Court of Odessa of 15 May 2009.
On 16 July 2009 the Odessa Regional Court of Appeal ruled in the presence of the applicant and his representative.
On 16 July 2009 the Odessa Regional Court of Appeal upheld the decision of the Prymorsky District Court of Odessa of 15 May 2009.
The applicant has not paid the fine of 170 Ukrainian hryvnias (UAH) imposed by the Prymorsky District Court of Odessa.
By a letter dated 17 March 2009, the Odessa City Council informed the applicant that holding a picket with such short notice was liable to be considered unlawful.

The Odessa City Council's letter of 17 March 2009 indicated that, pursuant to the Decree of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet of the USSR of 28 July 1988 on the procedure for organisation and holding of meetings, rallies, street marches and demonstrations in the USSR (the 1988 Decree), notification had to be given no later than ten days prior to the meeting in question.

The Odessa City Council's letter of 17 March 2009 indicated that the Constitutional Court of Ukraine, in its decision of 19 April 2001, had held that the organisers of peaceful assemblies must inform the authorities in advance of their intention to hold a meeting.
The Odessa City Council's letter of 17 March 2009 mentioned that no implementing law in respect of the right to peaceful assembly had yet been enacted in Ukraine.

The Odessa City Council's letter of 17 March 2009 mentioned that the 1988 Decree (Decree of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet of the USSR of 28 July 1988 on the procedure for organisation and holding of meetings, rallies, street marches and demonstrations in the USSR) was still in force.

The Odessa City Council's letter of 17 March 2009 informed the applicant that untimely notification about the picket could be considered a violation of the procedure for holding meetings under paragraph 2 of the 1988 Decree (Decree of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet of the USSR of 28 July 1988).

The Odessa City Council's letter of 17 March 2009 informed the applicant that the person responsible for untimely notification could be held administratively liable under Article 185-1 of the Code of Administrative Offences.

The Prymorsky District Court of Odessa held that the applicant was in breach of Article 185-1 of the Code of Administrative Offences because he had not complied with the ten-day notification requirement.

The Prymorsky District Court of Odessa based its findings on the 1988 Decree (Decree of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet of the USSR of 28 July 1988), which provided that an application to hold an assembly had to be lodged with the relevant authority at least ten days in advance.

The Prymorsky District Court of Odessa referred to the decision of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine of 19 April 2001 and noted that the exact time-limits for notification were to be regulated by law.

The Prymorsky District Court of Odessa indicated that the 1988 Decree (Decree of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet of the USSR of 28 July 1988) was valid in Ukraine under the Resolution of the Ukrainian Parliament (Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine) on temporary application of certain legislative acts of the Soviet Union.

The Prymorsky District Court of Odessa pointed to the fact that the applicant had been informed by the Odessa City Council that the notification he had given was liable to be regarded as contrary to the requirements of the legislation and had been warned that he could incur administrative liability.

In his appeal of 25 May 2009, the applicant argued that the 1988 Decree (Decree of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet of the USSR of 28 July 1988), on which the first-instance court had based its decision, was invalid and contrary to the Constitution of Ukraine.

In his appeal of 25 May 2009, the applicant noted that the 1988 Decree provided that persons wishing to hold a peaceful assembly had to seek permission, whereas the Constitution of Ukraine provided only that the authorities had to be notified of an intention to hold such an assembly.
In his appeal of 25 May 2009, the applicant noted that Article 92 of the Constitution of Ukraine provided that human rights guarantees had to be regulated exclusively by laws.

In his appeal of 25 May 2009, the applicant noted that Article 39 of the Constitution of Ukraine provided that restrictions on the right to peaceful assembly could be established only by law, whereas the 1988 Decree was not a law of Ukraine.
In his appeal of 25 May 2009, the applicant noted that at the time of the picket there had been no judicial decision restricting the picket as required by Article 39 of the Constitution of Ukraine.
Article 22 of the Constitution of Ukraine provides that human and citizens' rights and freedoms affirmed by the Constitution are not exhaustive.
Article 22 of the Constitution of Ukraine provides that constitutional rights and freedoms are guaranteed and shall not be abolished.

Article 22 of the Constitution of Ukraine provides that the content and scope of existing rights and freedoms shall not be diminished by the enactment of new laws or the amendment of laws that are in force.

Article 39 of the Constitution of Ukraine provides that citizens have the right to assemble peacefully without arms and to hold meetings, rallies, marches and demonstrations, after notifying the executive authorities and bodies of local self-government beforehand.

Article 39 of the Constitution of Ukraine provides that restrictions on the exercise of the right to peaceful assembly may be established by a court in accordance with the law, in the interests of national security and public order only, for the purpose of preventing disturbances or crimes, protecting the health of the population, or protecting the rights and freedoms of other persons.

Article 92(1) of the Constitution of Ukraine provides that human and citizens' rights and freedoms, the guarantees of these rights and freedoms, and the main duties of the citizen are determined exclusively by the laws of Ukraine.

Chapter XV (Transitional Provisions) of the Constitution of Ukraine provides that laws and other normative acts enacted prior to the entry into force of the Constitution shall apply in so far as they do not conflict with the Constitution of Ukraine.

Article 185-1 of the Code of Administrative Offences provides that a breach of the procedure for organising and holding meetings, rallies, street marches and demonstrations shall be punishable by a reprimand or by a fine of between ten and twenty-five times the minimum monthly wage.

Article 185-1 of the Code of Administrative Offences provides that the same actions committed within a year of the application of administrative penalties or by the organiser of the meeting, rally, street procession or demonstration shall be punishable by a fine of between twenty and one hundred times the minimum monthly wage, or by correctional labour of one to two months with a deduction of 20% of earnings, or by administrative detention of up to fifteen days.
Article 285 of the Code of Administrative Offences provides that a decision regarding an administrative offence shall be pronounced immediately after the examination of the case.
Article 285 of the Code of Administrative Offences provides that within three days a copy of the decision regarding an administrative offence shall be given or sent to the person concerned.

The Decree of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet of the USSR of 28 July 1988 on the procedure for organising and holding meetings, rallies, street marches and demonstrations in the USSR (the 1988 Decree) lays down the procedure for seeking and granting permission to organise and hold meetings, rallies, street marches and demonstrations.

The 1988 Decree provides that an application to hold a meeting, rally, street procession or demonstration shall be submitted to the executive committee of the appropriate local Soviet of people's deputies.

The 1988 Decree provides that an application to hold a meeting, rally, street procession or demonstration shall be submitted in writing no later than ten days before the planned date of the event in question.

The 1988 Decree provides that the executive committee of the Soviet of people's deputies shall examine the application and notify the representatives (organisers) of its decision no later than five days prior to the date of the event mentioned in the application.

The 1988 Decree provides that the executive committee of the Soviet of people's deputies shall ban a meeting, rally, street procession or demonstration if the goal of the event is contrary to the Constitution of the USSR, the constitutions of the Republics of the Union or of the autonomous republics, or poses a threat to public order and the safety of citizens.

The Resolution of the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine of 12 September 1991 on temporary application of certain legislative acts of the Soviet Union provides that, before the relevant legislation of Ukraine is enacted, the legislation of the USSR is applicable within the territory of Ukraine in respect of issues that have not been regulated by the legislation of Ukraine and in so far as they do not contravene the Constitution and legislation of Ukraine.

In its decision of 19 April 2001, the Constitutional Court of Ukraine considered an application by the Ministry of the Interior of Ukraine for an official interpretation of the provisions of Article 39 of the Constitution of Ukraine regarding timely notification to executive authorities or bodies of local self-government of planned meetings, rallies, marches or demonstrations.

The Constitutional Court of Ukraine's decision of 19 April 2001 noted that the current legislation of Ukraine does not provide for a specific time-limit within which the executive authorities or bodies of local self-government are to be notified about planned meetings, rallies, marches or demonstrations.

In its decision of 19 April 2001, the Constitutional Court of Ukraine held that the provisions of Article 39 of the Constitution of Ukraine on timely notification to executive authorities or bodies of local self-government about planned meetings, rallies, marches or demonstrations shall be understood to mean that organisers must inform the above-mentioned authorities in advance, that is, within a reasonable time prior to the date of the planned event.

The Constitutional Court of Ukraine's decision of 19 April 2001 held that the notification time-limits should not restrict the right of citizens under Article 39 of the Constitution of Ukraine, but should serve as a guarantee of this right and at the same time provide the relevant executive authorities or bodies of local self-government with an opportunity to take measures to ensure that citizens may freely hold meetings, rallies, marches and demonstrations and to protect public order and the rights and freedoms of others.

The Constitutional Court of Ukraine's decision of 19 April 2001 held that specifying the exact deadlines for timely notification with regard to the particularities of different forms of peaceful assembly, the number of participants, the venue, and the time of the event is a matter for legislative regulation.

On 21 May 2012 the Plenary of the Higher Administrative Court of Ukraine, by its Decree No. 6, decided to send the Information Note of April 2012 on a study and summary of the jurisprudence of administrative courts applying the relevant legislation and deciding cases concerning the exercise of the right to peaceful assembly in 2010 and 2011 for information to the judges of lower administrative courts.

The Information Note of April 2012 of the Higher Administrative Court of Ukraine stated that judicial practice contained instances of cases restricting the right to peaceful assembly being decided on the basis of the procedure for organising and holding meetings, rallies, street marches and demonstrations laid down by the Decree of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet of the USSR of 28 July 1988 No. 9306-XI, and that this approach is incorrect.

The Information Note of April 2012 of the Higher Administrative Court of Ukraine stated that the norms of the 1988 Decree establish the procedure for authorising (registering) peaceful assembly and empower the authorities and bodies of local self-government to ban such events, whereas the norms of the Constitution of Ukraine provide for a procedure whereby the authorities are notified that a gathering is to be held and provide that only the courts have power to ban a peaceful gathering.

The Information Note of April 2012 of the Higher Administrative Court of Ukraine stated that the 1988 Decree (Decree of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet of the USSR of 28 July 1988) should not be applied by courts when deciding cases concerning the right to peaceful assembly.

In a judgment of 30 March 2007 in the case of S. v. the Executive Committee of the Dnipropetrovs'k City Council, the Babushkinsky District Court of Dnipropetrovs'k held that the procedures for exercising the right to freedom of assembly and the procedures and grounds for restricting the right were not regulated by Ukrainian legislation.

In its judgment of 30 March 2007 in the case of S. v. the Executive Committee of the Dnipropetrovs'k City Council, the Babushkinsky District Court of Dnipropetrovs'k held that the Dnipropetrovs'k City Council had no grounds for adopting the impugned regulation on holding mass events in the city of Dnipropetrovs'k, which would interfere with the rights of citizens.

In a judgment of 29 November 2011, the Kyiv Administrative Court restricted the right of several non-governmental organisations and private persons to hold a demonstration on account, in particular, of their failure to notify the Kyiv City State Administration of their intention ten days in advance.
In its judgment of 29 November 2011, the Kyiv Administrative Court referred to the 1988 Decree (Decree of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet of the USSR of 28 July 1988).
The participants in the demonstration appealed against the Kyiv Administrative Court's judgment of 29 November 2011.
On 16 May 2012 the Kyiv Administrative Court of Appeal quashed the judgment of the Kyiv Administrative Court of 29 November 2011.

In its decision of 16 May 2012, the Kyiv Administrative Court of Appeal noted that the 1988 Decree conflicted with the Constitution of Ukraine as it required the organisers to seek permission to hold a demonstration and authorised the executive authorities to ban such an event, whereas Article 39 of the Constitution of Ukraine provided that the authorities should be notified that a demonstration was being planned and empowered only the judicial authorities to place restrictions on the organisation thereof.

In its decision of 16 May 2012, the Kyiv Administrative Court of Appeal noted that in its decision of 19 April 2001 the Constitutional Court of Ukraine had not referred to the 1988 Decree as a normative act which should apply in Ukraine to the legal relations under consideration.

In its decision of 16 May 2012, the Kyiv Administrative Court of Appeal noted that the file contained no documents proving that notification about the demonstration less than 10 days in advance had not allowed the police to ensure public order during the demonstration and that the holding of such an event could create a real risk of riots or crimes or endanger the health of the population and imperil the rights and freedoms of others.

In its decision of 16 May 2012, the Kyiv Administrative Court of Appeal concluded that the judgment of the Kyiv Administrative Court of 29 November 2011 was incompatible with Article 39 of the Constitution of Ukraine and Article 11 of the Convention.

In a decision of 11 October 2012, the Kyiv Administrative Court of Appeal quashed a judgment of the Kyiv Administrative Court which had restricted the freedom of peaceful assembly in respect of a number of political and non-governmental organisations upon an application by the Kyiv City State Administration.

In its decision of 11 October 2012, the Kyiv Administrative Court of Appeal noted that in deciding the case the first-instance court (Kyiv Administrative Court) had had regard to the provisions of the 1988 Decree (Decree of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet of the USSR of 28 July 1988), whereas since 1996 the question of holding peaceful gatherings had been regulated by the Constitution of Ukraine.

In its decision of 11 October 2012, the Kyiv Administrative Court of Appeal stated that the 1988 Decree conflicted with the Constitution of Ukraine as it provided for a procedure for seeking permission to hold a demonstration.

In its decision of 11 October 2012, the Kyiv Administrative Court of Appeal stated that the 1988 Decree concerned the holding of demonstrations in a non-existent country (the USSR), regulated relations between the citizens of the USSR and the executive committees of the Soviets of People's Deputies, and considered demonstrations on the basis of their compatibility with the Constitution of the USSR and the constitutions of the union and autonomous republics, that is, non-existent constitutions of non-existent subjects.

In its decision of 11 October 2012, the Kyiv Administrative Court of Appeal noted that under the Constitution of Ukraine human rights and freedoms, and the relevant safeguards, could be defined only by the laws of Ukraine.

Other relevant domestic law and practice and relevant international documents concerning the right to peaceful assembly can be found in the case of Vyerentsov v. Ukraine (application no. 20372/11, paragraphs 26, 32, 33 and 38 to 43, judgment of 11 April 2013).
